title: Stargazers urged to watch Saturn's rings and the Leonid meteor shower
excerpt: The great square of Pegasus, along with Andromeda and Triangulum, remain prominent, while below the square, lower towards the southern horizon, the planet Saturn is well placed.
content:
Here's what you can see in the night sky in November.

The great square of Pegasus, along with Andromeda and Triangulum, remain prominent, while below the square, lower towards the southern horizon, the planet Saturn is well placed.

Saturn will appear to the naked eye as a dull yellowish object looking just like a bright star but, unlike the stars, planets don’t twinkle, making them a bit easier to spot.

A pair of binoculars is all that is needed to confirm it is not a point source like stars, but a telescope will show why it is the one object that, when seen for the first time, provides the ‘WOW’ factor.

The glory is in its system of rings, once seen, never forgotten.

High overhead is Cassiopeia, easy to spot as its five bright naked-eye stars form the letter ‘W’.

To its left is another bright constellation, Perseus; several of its members are naked-eye, one is Mirfak or Alpha Perseus.

This star is classed as a supergiant, and binoculars will bring out its yellowish/white colour.

Surrounding Mirfak in your field of view will be many other stars as they are members of a fine open cluster.

Some star atlases give this cluster other names such as Melotte 20 or Collinder 39.

Many of the stars will appear to you as coloured blue and are much hotter than our Sun, something like 50,000K.

The stars seen in your binoculars are thought to lie about 600 light-years away.

The constellation has much more to offer.

From Mirfak, halfway towards the two left-hand stars in Cassiopeia, is the famous ‘double’ cluster, yes, two clusters of stars side by side in the field of view.

They are further away – roughly 7,000 light-years and older, but they aren’t the same age; one is more than five million years old and the other a mere three million years old.

They are also known by another name, Caldwell 14, from a list thought up by the late great Sir Patrick Moore.

‘Caldwell’ was his middle name.

For our next target, go back to Mirfak.

From here is a line of stars falling roughly towards Triangulum.

Look for a naked-eye reddish star – this is Algol, also known as the ‘demon’ star.

Algol is not one, but a multiple-star system with at least three components, possibly more.

It acquired its sinister moniker because the ancient astronomers observed it change brightness, always remaining visible to the naked eye but apparently ‘winking’.

With hindsight and technology, we know the reason as the stars in this system orbit one another and, from time to time, one passes in front of the other, causing the bright component ‘Algol’ to appear less bright, or ‘wink’.

From Algol, move the binoculars slowly to the right and locate a much fainter open cluster M34.

Its age is thought to be around 200 million years, and it’s about 1,500 light-years from Earth.

From a dark site, it can just be made out with the naked eye; otherwise, a pair of binoculars will be required to see it.

There are some good photographic opportunities and chances to see other naked-eye planets and stars.

In the early hours of the 14th and 15th, the planets Jupiter and Mars appear close together in the constellation Leo.

On the 24th, the Moon appears between the Hyades and Pleiades star clusters in Taurus.

On the 29th and 30th, the Moon joins Jupiter and Mars in Leo.

The famous Leonid meteor shower peaks on the 18th and 19th.

The Moon will not interfere and is best before dawn when the radiant, located within the sickle of Leo, will be high in the sky.

The meteors are some of the fastest we see and can be very bright.

No optical aid required, just wrap up warm, lie back and watch the spectacle.

The Moon is full on the 24th, new on the 9th, and first quarter is on the 17th.
